import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 10

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/10](https://www.erdosproblems.com/10)
-/

namespace Erdos10

/--
The set of natural numbers that can be written as a sum
of a prime and at most $k$ powers of $2$.
-/
abbrev sumPrimeAndTwoPows (k : ℕ) : Set ℕ :=
  { p + (pows.map (2 ^ ·)).sum | (p : ℕ) (pows : Multiset ℕ) (_ : p.Prime)
    (_ : pows.card ≤ k)}

/--
Is there some $k$ such that every integer is the sum of a prime and at most $k$
powers of $2$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ k, sumPrimeAndTwoPows k = Set.univ \ {0, 1} := by
  sorry

/--
Gallagher [Ga75] has shown that for any $ϵ > 0$ there exists $k(ϵ)$
such that the set of integers which are the sum of a prime and at most $k(ϵ)$
many powers of $2$ has lower density at least $1 - ϵ$.

Ref: Gallagher, P. X., _Primes and powers of 2_.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.gallagher (ε : ℝ)
    (hε : 0 < ε) : ∃ k, 1 - ε ≤ (sumPrimeAndTwoPows k).lowerDensity := by
  sorry

/--
Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo98] have conjectured that at most $3$
powers of $2$ suffice for all odd integers, and hence at most $4$ powers of $2$
suffice for all even integers.

Ref: Granville, A. and Soundararajan, K., _A Binary Additive Problem of Erdős and the Order of $2$ mod $p^2$_
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.granville_soundararajan_odd :
    {n : ℕ | Odd n ∧ 1 < n} ⊆ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 3 ∧
      {n : ℕ | Even n ∧ n ≠ 0} ⊆ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 4 := by
  sorry

/--
Bogdan Grechuk has observed that `1117175146` is not the sum of a prime
and at most $3$ powers of $2$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.grechuk_example :
    1117175146 ∉ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 3 := by
  sorry

/--
There are infinitely many even integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.two_pows :
    Set.Infinite <| {n : ℕ | Even n} \ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 2 := by
  sorry

/--
Bogdan Grechuk has observed that $1117175146$ is not the sum of a prime and at most $3$
powers of $2$, and pointed out that parity considerations, coupled with the fact that there
are many integers not the sum of a prime and $2$ powers of $2$ suggest that there exist
infinitely many even integers which are not the sum of a prime and at most $3$ powers of $2$).
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_10.variants.grechuk :
    Set.Infinite <| {n : ℕ | Even n} \ sumPrimeAndTwoPows 3 := by
  sorry

end Erdos10

status_issues.source_status: The positive statement follows from Pan's 2009 preprint, published in 2011 and cited as a proved result by Problem 9. This is a corollary of Pan's construction, not an explicitly named Grechuk theorem in that paper. The available Problem 10 snapshot itself still phrases the conclusion as a suggestion.
status_issues.evidence: In §2 of https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.3809, Pan constructs ≫ε X^(1−ε) odd exceptions to p+2^a+2^b inside S = {n ≤ X : n ≡ β mod 2W}, where γ₀ = 3 divides W and β ≡ 0 mod γ₀. Consequently these exceptions, apart from n = 3, are composite. Such an n is also absent from sumPrimeAndTwoPows 2: zero powers would make n prime; one positive-exponent power can be split into two equal powers; and the remaining single-power case 2^0 forces the odd n to equal 3. If n+1 were an odd prime plus at most three powers, parity would force a 2^0 term; deleting it would represent n with at most two powers. Thus any remaining representation of n+1 must use prime 2. There are only O((log X)^3) such numbers up to X+1, negligible compared with Pan's count. Infinitely many even n+1 therefore remain unrepresented. The exact combinatorial reduction was independently proved in /workspace/review/parity.lean.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to research solved and cite Pan's construction with the parity/counting corollary. Retain the existing positive mathematical statement.

reformulations.difference: Lean requires one bound covering every natural number greater than 1. The May 2026 source snapshot asks for a bound covering every sufficiently large integer.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every member of sumPrimeAndTwoPows k is at least 2, so the set equality is equivalent to universal representability for n > 1. This implies eventual representability. Conversely, suppose k works for all n ≥ N. Take K = max k N. The original representations still use at most K powers, and every 2 ≤ n < N has the representation n = 2 + (n − 2) copies of 2^0, using at most N powers. Thus the finite initial segment can be absorbed by enlarging the bound. Both equivalences were proved in /workspace/review/boundaries.lean without using the file's sorry-backed theorems.

sources_consulted: https://arxiv.org/e-print/0905.3809 — read the LaTeX source, especially Theorem 1 and the construction and final counting estimate in §2.

review.notes: No mathematical misformalizations found in the definition or six theorem statements. Checked the multiset and empty-sum semantics, k = 0, exclusions of 0 and 1, density normalization and its zero denominator, quantifier/answer scope, and parity boundaries. A bounded exhaustive Lean computation confirmed the 1117175146 counterexample, including repeated and zero exponents. The live Erdős site returned Cloudflare challenges, so source comparison used the archived pages listed above; later site edits could not be checked. Gallagher's and Granville–Soundararajan's claims are explicit in the accessible Problem 10 remarks, although their primary full texts were inaccessible. The main equivalence and the status issue's combinatorial reduction compile without sorry dependencies; Pan's analytic estimate was not formalized. The file under review was not modified.
